mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting drained peat — blocking canals so the water table rises — works on the fuel. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is stated to reduce fire risk through increased moisture in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is given as a route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Most of the cell describes the hazard from the loss side and the engine reads rewetting as the reversal of that chain: drainage and degradation made peat vulnerable to fire (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1); cleared, drained and replanted peat domes become vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); the drier conditions following drainage increase the risk of fire (ev_wgy_ram_14); and in a hotter, drier European climate the risk of forest and peat fires in drained peatlands is expected to increase further (ev_wgy_qa_8). The one quantified result comes from a modelled fire-hazard index after large-scale canal-blocking rewetting in Riau, Sumatra: the frequency of continuous extreme-class hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1). Indonesian project accounts add field observations: in South Sumatra a revegetated project still survived large fires in 2015 and 2019, restoration in the area having restrained the spread of fires from nearby areas (ev_wet_fire_budi20_1); and in Riau 312 canal blocks over 6,060 ha of community land restored the hydrology of the peatland system and reduced the risk of wildfires (ev_wet_fire_terz22_1).
caveats: The drainage-fire chain is asserted, not measured. The two newest statements come from advocacy-adjacent sources — a question-and-answer brief drafted for the EU Nature Restoration Law negotiations (ev_wgy_qa_8) and the Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting (ev_wgy_ram_14) — and the others from an introductory book chapter (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1) and a Ramsar briefing note (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); none measures fire before and after rewetting. The two restoration-frame claims are hedged as potential benefits, and Ritzema's is attributed to other studies rather than measured (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). The quantified study models hazard from weather data checked against satellite hotspots, not burned area, and its other results are weaker or opposite: the area under extreme-class hazard was only 5% lower after rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2); the mean duration of extreme events increased, with widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurring only in the drying El Niño years of 2015 and 2019 (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3); and the authors conclude that duration was controlled by the weather and not influenced by rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4). In the severe dry years, when the widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurred, no benefit is visible. The authors also caution that La Niña years drive part of the decline, so the rewetting effect may be overstated. Provenance: Indonesian and Malaysian humid-tropical peat in upper-middle-income settings, plus guidance statements with no site; nothing was measured in a low-income or lower-middle-income country, and the benefit lands on the landscape and on society, not on a farmer's plot. The Indonesian project accounts carry no comparison area: the surviving Sumatran site is a single-site observation on land the authors describe as never fully rewetted (ev_wet_fire_budi20_1), and the Riau canal-block claim reports no fire data and comes from authors that include project staff (ev_wet_fire_terz22_1). The same Sumatran source records the other side at a neighbouring agro-sylvofishery project: trade-offs are increasing the vulnerability of peatland to fire, almost 50% of the area burned in the 2019 El Nino, and the causes of the fires are still being argued (ev_wet_fire_budi20_2) - a measured harm kept in the row, tied by the authors to liming peat for dryland crops and a fishery canal rather than to rewetting as such.

mitigation_mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). Stage is the other half of the story — the same floodplain roughness that trims the downstream peak can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up) — and timing is a third thing again: the gully whose peak fell by 49% also responded faster, its lag between rainfall and peak discharge shortening (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
caveats: Catchment scale and extreme events are the unproven part. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment in the best-monitored UK test (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null); the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null); monitoring cannot isolate a restoration effect from catchment storm-flow data at all (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable); and the evidence does not suggest a major difference to downstream flood risk at large catchment scales, or for the most extreme events (ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null, ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null). During major catastrophic floods the whole basin may be saturated and the presence, absence or management of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null). The sign also flips with position: an on-site storage gain can still produce an increase in flood peaks at catchment scale through flood-wave synchrony (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff partially synchronised sub-catchment peaks and so increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); restoring the wrong reach worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects and in some scenarios raised aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); and moving the same project downstream along the channel turned a 14% peak reduction into about a 1% increase (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_4). Rewetting also consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — the empty space a flood would fill is exactly what an ecological water-level target removes. Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. The state-dependence statements (ev_wgy_ram_10, ev_wgy_ram_11, ev_wgy_ram_12) are guidance-level synthesis, two with their own references and one an expert assertion; they establish that the sign depends on the peat's starting state, on top of its catchment position, but not how often each case occurs. The 30% review average credits the whole river-and-floodplain bundle - river restoration, floodplain and wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage - not wetland restoration alone; it is a peak, not a stage, figure from a corpus that is mostly European and largely British, and its statement that the reduction is larger in larger catchments sits against the catchment-scale nulls above (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Provenance: this is a temperate, high-income corpus, UK and US catchments almost without exception, with no measured low-income or lower-middle-income result in scope; and the benefit is off the farm, arriving at downstream receptors rather than on the plot.

mitigation_mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. Wave heights fall by 72% across salt marsh, with a 95% confidence interval of 62 to 79% in a meta-analysis of field measurements (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1); up to 82% of wave energy is dissipated over marsh against 29% over the adjacent sand flat (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_3); storm-surge attenuation rates run from 1.7 to 25 cm per kilometre of marsh depending on marsh and storm characteristics (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_1). The vegetated-versus-unvegetated contrast is consistent — salt marsh vegetation had a significant positive effect on wave attenuation, and every paired study comparing vegetated marsh with intertidal mudflat concluded attenuation is greater over the marsh (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_1, ev_flood_hazard_shep11_2). Farmland gives a further view: on the Queensland coast after a cyclone, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes experienced lower surface water presence compared with more distant areas (ev_flood_hazard_rowl26w1_1).
caveats: What has been measured is wave attenuation under ordinary conditions: the meta-analysed measurements are all taken under normal conditions of low waves (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1). The function weakens exactly where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). Floodwater attenuation inside the marsh, meaning flood-peak reduction and floodwater storage, has never been quantified: the systematic review found no study evaluating it (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_5). Siting can cancel the benefit, since levees and dikes behind a marsh cause water to set up against the structure and limit the surge-attenuating effect (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_4). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). The Queensland result is an association around existing mangrove and tidal marsh together, read from a satellite surface-water index that does not separate surge from rain flooding; the authors say it does not provide direct evidence of causal protection, and the binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to their models (ev_flood_hazard_rowl26w1_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on Australian, US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm, apart from the Queensland cropland result.

mitigation_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). Restoration changed the timing and the peak of delivery but not the volume: the runoff coefficient was unchanged at both restored sites (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.

No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting raises the water table in the peat, and the water does not stop at the project boundary. The Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting sets two design constraints on this: where adjacent land use may be impaired, rewetting must be done gradually and flooding of surrounding land must be avoided (ev_wgy_ram_15); and where downward seepage is diffuse, elevating the water table in a residual peat massif will require raising the water level in the surrounding land, farmland included (ev_wgy_ram_16). The first treats waterlogging of neighbouring land as a risk to be managed; the second describes a setting where wetting neighbouring farmland is built into the method.
caveats: These are design constraints stated by an authority, not measurements. Neither statement says how often neighbouring land is waterlogged, by how much, for how long, or what it costs the farmers who work it, and both come from one advocacy-adjacent guidance document; they establish that the risk is recognised, not its size or frequency, and they should not be read as evidence that rewetting routinely floods farmland. Unlike the flood benefits elsewhere in this recipe, the cost here falls on the neighbouring farm household rather than downstream. For scoping, a rewetting proposal adjacent to farmland should plan for gradual water-level raising, identify the adjacent parcels whose water level the design may depend on, and treat any need to raise water on those parcels as something to agree with their users before the works, not an incidental side effect. No country, income group, climate zone or farming system is attached to either statement.

mitigation_mechanism: Drought damages the restored wetland by taking away the water it runs on. In a rewetted Indonesian peat restoration area, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). The authors read their long record as showing that a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface, with carbon-emission spikes, even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and remaining peat-swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6). On a restored floodplain the hazard works by removing the flood the wetland depends on: in 2020, lack of snow cover and severe drought meant no spring flooding on the Pripyat floodplain, and migrating and nesting birds on the restored floodplain meadows declined strongly (ev_wgy_blr_6). The Ramsar technical guidance records, from its authors' knowledge, that a large number of planted areas in degraded tropical peat-swamp forest have been lost to drought, as well as to fire, flooding and out-competition by ferns and sedges (ev_wgy_ram_22).
caveats: Two of the four units are measurements — subsidence in Sumatra and bird numbers in a Belarus project evaluation; the other two are interpretation: the Hooijer authors' reading of their own record, and an expert statement with no frequency, site or measurement, made where the guidance itself notes there is very little literature on what happens after planting. Design implication: a wetland investment in a drought-prone setting should budget and monitor for drought-year losses of peat surface, carbon, plantings and habitat function rather than treat them as failure of the works, and should expect the asset to deliver least in the dry years.

mitigation_mechanism: What wears a salt marsh away is the ordinary wave climate, not the cyclone. A global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements found that most salt-marsh deterioration is caused by moderate storms of monthly frequency (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6), while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion rates (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5) — the marsh survives the violent event and is eroded between them.
caveats: Both units are drawn from the same sentence of the same review reporting the same global dataset, so this is a single line of evidence. It concerns lateral erosion of the marsh edge and no other failure mode, and it describes established marsh rather than a newly planted or recently restored one, where edge stability is likely to be weakest. The review's accompanying point is that retreat scales with wave energy rather than switching on above a critical storm, so the maintenance burden is continuous rather than event-driven: budget for steady edge retreat under the everyday wave climate rather than for post-cyclone repair. Provenance is high-income North Atlantic and European coasts.

mitigation_mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.
